title: Josiah's Great Passover and His Death at Megiddo
summary: Josiah keeps a Passover in Jerusalem so carefully ordered and so generously supplied that none like it had been held since the days of Samuel. Thirteen years later, when Pharaoh Neco of Egypt marches north toward the Euphrates, Josiah goes out to stop him, ignoring Neco's warning that God had sent him. Josiah is shot by archers at Megiddo, dies in Jerusalem, and is mourned by all Judah and lamented by Jeremiah.
story: Chapter 34 ended with the covenant renewed; this chapter shows that covenant kept in worship. Josiah's Passover is the high point of the reform and the last great festival in the story of the kings. Then, with a single phrase, “After all this” (verse 20), the tone changes. The king who listened so well to the book fails to listen to a word from an unexpected mouth, and he dies in a battle he did not need to fight. With Josiah's death, the last faithful king of Judah is gone. The next chapter moves swiftly through four weak kings to the fall of Jerusalem.
historical:
The Passover took place in Josiah's eighteenth year, commonly dated 622 BC. Josiah's death came in 609 BC. By then Assyria had lost Nineveh (612 BC) and was making a last stand in northern Mesopotamia, and Egypt under Pharaoh Neco II marched north to support its old rival against the rising power of Babylon. 2 Kings 23:29 reports the event very briefly. Josiah's motive for intercepting Neco is not stated; many historians think he hoped to prevent an Egyptian-Assyrian recovery that would threaten Judah's newfound independence. Megiddo guarded a key pass on the coastal route north, and the Plain of Megiddo (the Jezreel Valley) was the site of many battles.

Carchemish, on the Euphrates, was a major crossing and later the site of the decisive battle in 605 BC in which Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon defeated the Egyptians. Josiah's death opened Judah to Egyptian control; Neco would soon depose his successor (36:3). The prophet Zechariah later compares a great mourning to the mourning in the plain of Megiddo (Zechariah 12:11), which many interpreters connect with the grief over Josiah.
cultural:
Passover was originally a household meal (Exodus 12) and by Josiah's time had become a national feast at the central sanctuary (Deuteronomy 16:5-6). The Levites slaughtered, skinned, and distributed the animals so that families could eat, and the king and officials donated tens of thousands of animals so that the poor could take part. The Passover lambs were roasted as the law required, while other holy offerings were boiled and shared as fellowship meals.

The instruction to put the ark in the temple (verse 3) is puzzling, since the ark had been placed there by Solomon. Some think it had been removed during Manasseh's reign or during the repairs; others read the verse as a way of saying the Levites no longer needed to carry it and should turn to their other duties. This is the last mention of the ark in the historical books. Kings in battle sometimes disguised themselves to avoid being targeted, as Ahab did at Ramoth-gilead (18:29). Laments for fallen kings were a recognized form of poetry; the Book of Laments mentioned in verse 25 is lost and is not the same as the biblical book of Lamentations, which mourns the fall of Jerusalem.
literary: The chapter has two unequal parts: a long, detailed Passover (verses 1-19) and a brief, sudden death (verses 20-27). The Passover section repeats the verb prepare again and again, stressing order and readiness; everything is done according to Moses, David, and the king's command. The death scene deliberately echoes the death of Ahab in chapter 18: a king disguises himself, goes to battle against a prophetic warning, is struck by archers, and says to his driver or servants that he is wounded. The echo is sobering. Josiah, the best of the later kings, dies in the manner of the northern kingdom's most notorious king, because he “did not listen” to the words “from the mouth of God” (verse 22).

outline.t: Josiah prepares the priests and Levites
The king and officials provide the offerings
The Passover and Feast of Unleavened Bread celebrated
Josiah confronts Neco and dies at Megiddo

doctrines.note: The Passover gathers the whole people with each group in its role: king and officials giving, priests and Levites serving, singers and gatekeepers at their posts. Ordered, generous, shared worship is the fruit of renewed covenant.
God speaks to Josiah through the mouth of a foreign king. The chapter warns that God's word may come through unexpected voices and must be weighed, not dismissed because of its source.
The best king of the age dies young in battle. Chronicles does not soften the shock; it records the nation's grief and makes lament part of Israel's life.

words.note: Pesach, Passover. The name comes from the verb for passing over (Exodus 12:13), when the LORD spared the houses marked with blood. Used thirteen times here, it frames the chapter as a remembrance of the exodus, God's founding act of rescue.

Kun, to prepare or establish. It recurs through the Passover account (verses 4, 6, 14, 15, 16, and more): prepare yourselves, the service was prepared. The repetition stresses that Josiah's worship was carefully ordered and ready.

Chaphas, a verb that usually means to search, but in the reflexive form used here means to disguise oneself. The same verb describes Ahab's disguise before his fatal battle (18:29). Its use here ties Josiah's end to Ahab's.
Qun, to chant a lament. Jeremiah's laments over Josiah and the singers' ongoing laments show that grief for the king became part of Israel's memory and worship.

christ: Passover is the feast most tied to Christ in the New Testament. Jesus celebrated it with his disciples on the night before his death, gave the bread and cup new meaning as his body and blood (Luke 22:14-20), and died as the true Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7). Josiah's death also stands in the background of the Gospels' picture of mourning for a pierced king: Zechariah 12:10-11, which compares a great lament to the mourning at Megiddo, is applied in John 19:37 to the crucified Jesus. Unlike Josiah, whose death ended hope for his kingdom, Jesus' death was followed by resurrection. The links are the New Testament's own readings, and they turn Judah's lament into a pointer toward a greater grief and a greater joy.

hard.q: Huldah promised that Josiah would go to his grave in peace (34:28). How does that fit his violent death in battle?
hard.a: Huldah's promise explained itself: Josiah's eyes would not see the calamity coming on Jerusalem. In that sense it was kept; he died before the Babylonian conquest and was buried in his fathers' tomb with national mourning. Many interpreters read peace in that light, as dying before the judgment and receiving honorable burial. Others see the promise as conditional on Josiah's continued obedience and note that the Chronicler blames his death on his refusal to listen to God's word through Neco. A related puzzle is that God spoke through a pagan king; Chronicles presents this matter-of-factly, and 2 Chronicles 36:22-23 will show God moving another foreign king, Cyrus. Both explanations take the text seriously; the second fits the Chronicler's pattern of explaining a king's end by his response to God's word.

questions: Josiah's Passover was generous, ordered, and joyful. What would it take for worship in your community to be marked by all three?
Josiah did not listen to God's word because it came from an unlikely source. When have you missed a true word because you disliked the messenger?
Judah made lament for Josiah part of its ongoing life. How do you and your community make room for grief in faith?
